exercises.title: Keep useful text
exercises.why: A tiny, reliable transformation is useful when checking data before an AI tool call.
exercises.brief: Read the complete `keep_positive` example, then write `keep_nonempty` by copying its loop shape. Keep strings whose length is greater than zero, in encounter order. Run the tests after writing the one function.
hints: Start with an empty result list.
Loop over each value and append only when the condition is true.
Return the result after the loop.

exercises.title: Keep longer text
exercises.why: Filtering short labels is a practical first check before passing user input to an AI workflow.
exercises.brief: Implement `keep_long_enough(values)`. Return the strings with at least three characters, preserving encounter order. Empty strings and one or two character strings are discarded. Write one small function and use the tests to guide your repair loop.
hints: The boundary is inclusive: length three stays.
Build a new list as you visit each string.
An empty input naturally returns an empty list.

exercises.title: Count event names
exercises.why: Counting repeated events is a small foundation for inspecting AI pipeline outcomes.
exercises.brief: Read the worked `count_fruit` loop, then implement `count_events(names)` with the same dictionary pattern. Count each event string and keep first-seen key order. Use `counts.get(name, 0) + 1`, run the tests, and repair one failure at a time.
hints: Each name needs its old count plus one.
Return the dictionary after the loop.

exercises.title: Count word endings
exercises.why: A derived count mirrors simple telemetry summaries used to understand an AI system's behavior.
exercises.brief: Implement `count_final_chars(words)`. For every non-empty word, count its final character. Ignore empty words, preserve the dictionary's first-seen key order, and return an empty dictionary when no words contribute. Write one function and use the tests to find the next small correction.
hints: Skip a word when its length is zero.
The final character is selected with `word[-1]`.
Update a dictionary count just like a tally.
